name: Fandango
lede: Fandango is a strong reddish purple named for the Spanish dance, recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary and still listed as an X11 web color today.

sections.title: Named for a dance, dated to 1925
sections.body: Wikipedia's account of Fandango, citing Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, dates the name's first recorded use to 1925, on plate 52, swatch L10 [1]. The ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 places the hue in block 254, calling the region vivid purplish red, Munsell notation 2.8RP 4.4/14.1 [2]. The dance that gives the color its name is a lively, partnered Spanish and Portuguese form, but no source consulted here explains why this particular shade took the dance's name [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[red-violet]], [[maximum-red-purple]], [[red-violet-crayola]] and [[rhodamine-purple]], at 3.6, 3.9, 4.5 and 4.8 ΔE [1]. Fandango sits brighter and more saturated than the dull reddish purples on, and [[magenta]] than to true red [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This hue is rare in our archive of 23,781 paintings: a match within six units covers at least five percent of the canvas in only 3 of them, all from a single early-1900s group of Indian devotional works, as photographed [4]. The small sample sits entirely in shadow regions of those paintings [4]. A count this low supports no claim about painters or periods beyond that one group [4].

origin.named_after: the fandango, a Spanish and Portuguese partnered dance; the link between dance and color is undocumented here
